subject: compensatory heterogeneity and finite mixture models

messages.author: 2c49652a5796ed9c
messages.subject: compensatory heterogeneity and finite mixture models
parts:
I'm seeking some feedback on some observations regarding compensatory heterogeneity and finite mixture models.  I came across
Howe et al. 2013 yesterday which shows strong evidence for heterogeneity in g0 and sigma and modelling this heterogeneity as finite mixtures substantially raises estimated densities.  The link to that paper is here:

http://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10144-013-0389-y

In light of Murray's recent paper on compensatory heterogeneity, I thought I'd compare finite mixture models using the different parameterizations on some male black bear SCR data I have.  Murray's paper can be found here:

http://www.otago.ac.nz/density/pdfs/Efford%20and%20Mowat%202014%20Ecology.pdf

My initial thought was that we can test for non-compensatory heterogeneity in g0 using the a0 parameterization and it may be that Howe et al. could have gotten by using only a finite mixture on sigma and the a0 parameterization.  Here is an AIC table for a model without heterogeneity and 5 possible ways to model heterogeneity.  I've varied starting values and can't get different estimates, so I don't think any of these are at a local maxima and the mixture proportions aren't estimated on a boundary for any of these models.


                                                 model   detectfn npar    logLik      AIC     AICc  dAICc AICcwt
modMh5 D~Area a0~Area + bk + h2 sigma~Area + h2 pmix~h2 halfnormal   10 -1158.844 2337.687 2340.105  0.000 0.8268
modMh4      D~Area a0~Area + bk + h2 sigma~Area pmix~h2 halfnormal    9 -1162.646 2343.292 2345.248  5.143 0.0632
modMh1      D~Area g0~Area + bk + h2 sigma~Area pmix~h2 halfnormal    9 -1162.706 2343.412 2345.368  5.263 0.0595
modMh3 D~Area g0~Area + bk + h2 sigma~Area + h2 pmix~h2 halfnormal   10 -1162.002 2344.003 2346.421  6.316 0.0351
modMh6      D~Area a0~Area + bk sigma~Area + h2 pmix~h2 halfnormal    9 -1164.063 2346.125 2348.082  7.977 0.0153
modMh2      D~Area g0~Area + bk sigma~Area + h2 pmix~h2 halfnormal    9 -1168.716 2355.432 2357.388 17.283 0.0000
modM                     D~Area g0~Area + bk sigma~Area halfnormal    7 -1183.127 2380.254 2381.446 41.341 0.0000

We see that 1) Heterogeneity of some sort is strongly supported, 2) the best g0 parameterization has a finite mixture on both g0 and sigma as in Howe et al., 3) among the models with a finite mixture on sigma alone, the one with compensatory heterogeneity on a0 is strongly preferred (modMh2 vs. modMh6), 4)  the two models with a finite mixture on either a0 or g0 alone are nearly indistinguishable and 5)  The model with finite mixtures on a0 and sigma is strongly preferred, suggesting non-compensatory heterogeneity on a0.

Now, let's look at the estimates and standard errors for N at one of the sites.

M:  64 (10)
Mh1:  106 (47)
Mh2:  155 (38)
Mh3:  200 (85)
Mh4:  108 (43)
Mh5:  79 (18)
Mh6:  55 (9)

We see that 1) The compensatory heterogeneity model (Mh6) produces a slightly lower estimate as the base model (M) with a similar standard error.  This seems consistent with Murray's points about what happens when you ignore heterogeneity that is compensatory.  2)  The top model with non-compensatory heterogeneity (Mh5) produces estimates that are slightly higher than the base model (M) but the standard error is much larger.  3)  The model fit by Howe et al. (Mh3) has produces a very large and imprecise estimate, but luckily, it doesn't carry much support.  Should we expect the estimates from models Mh5 and Mh3 to differ this greatly?

Let's look at the coefficients of these two models to see what is going on:

> coef(modMh5)
                   beta    SE.beta        lcl         ucl
D            -6.4536772 0.24774184 -6.9392423 -5.96811207
D.AreaPB     -0.5528546 0.25927280 -1.0610199 -0.04468924
a0            6.0425960 0.16944474  5.7104904  6.37470157
a0.AreaPB    -0.6834435 0.26055073 -1.1941135 -0.17277344
a0.bk         1.0841709 0.18395220  0.7236312  1.44471058
a0.h22       -1.2594503 0.36813108 -1.9809740 -0.53792665
sigma         8.0558197 0.09371943  7.8721330  8.23950644
sigma.AreaPB -0.5720924 0.13259523 -0.8319743 -0.31221055
sigma.h22     0.9389699 0.24047476  0.4676480  1.41029177
pmix.h22      1.0072750 0.37571976  0.2708778  1.74367221

> coef(modMh3)
                   beta   SE.beta        lcl          ucl
D            -5.9757480 0.3957638 -6.7514309 -5.200065229
D.AreaPB     -0.1057174 0.2684513 -0.6318723  0.420437443
g0           -2.6879640 0.1724324 -3.0259254 -2.350002747
g0.AreaPB    -0.1776700 0.2549628 -0.6773880  0.322047930
g0.bk         1.2809791 0.1896395  0.9092925  1.652665767
g0.h22       -1.5156360 0.5264688 -2.5474959 -0.483776057
sigma         8.1066234 0.1014152  7.9078531  8.305393563
sigma.AreaPB -0.2620560 0.1308774 -0.5185710 -0.005540901
sigma.h22    -0.6996332 0.3035928 -1.2946641 -0.104602325
pmix.h22      1.8856367 0.4507021  1.0022767  2.768996601



The a0 parameterization has the second mixture group increasing sigma, but reducing a0, which implies g0 is reduced, and more than you would expect with compensatory heterogeneity.  The g0 parameterization has the second group decreasing both sigma and g0, or conversely, the first group increases g0 as you increase sigma, the same pattern observed by Howe et al., the opposite of what is observed using a0, and completely inconsistent with compensatory heterogeneity.

This leads me wondering 1)  Maybe the a0 parameterization is better for modelling individual heterogeneity and Howe et al. may find that this model fits their data better, produces lower and less variable estimates, and their cause for concern about modelling individual heterogeneity was perhaps exaggerated, 2) maybe we need to allow for different mixture proportions on the two parameters, or 3) these finite mixture models are just not reliable, or at least not reliable with my small data set.

A just so story for my top model is that we sampled during breeding season so subordinate males moved more than dominant  males (larger sigma) and subordinate males are smaller so they tend to leave less hair in the hair snares (lower g0).  I'm sure I could think of some more!

Thoughts?

Thanks for your time (if you made it this far!),

Ben Augustine

messages.author: 118cea91a1619106
messages.subject: Re: compensatory heterogeneity and finite mixture models
parts:
Hi Ben
It's a challenge to disentangle what is going on here.I haven't dived into the meat of the issue yet, but I've two minor comments: 1. Your models are fully area-specific in all parameters except pmix, so it would be faster and probably more interpretable to fit one area at a time. 2. If it weren't for bk and using detectfn HN instead of HHN ((halfnormal g instead of lambda) I would expect Mh1 to be the same as Mh4 and Mh3 to be the same as Mh5. The difference in maximized LL between Mh3 and Mh5 is a worry - maybe the maximization got stuck on a local peak (see secr-finitemixtures.pdf)?

I have the feeling that neither the a0 parameterization nor finite mixtures are entirely safe to use. I see the a0 parameterization as a 'work in progress'  - it doesn't really make sense when the number or arrangement of detectors varies, and may fail in other situations.
Murray

messages.author: 0dbfcf0efe4ff8fe
messages.subject: Re: compensatory heterogeneity and finite mixture models
parts:
Hi Ben,

In Howe et al. (2013), we presented results for females only.  If you are analyzing a data set that includes both sexes, then I wouldn't expect the patterns of variation in SECR model parameters to be similar, as sex is likely a large source of the individual heterogeneity (especially in sigma) in your data set.  As I understand it, the a0 formulation and a two-point mixture distribution is well-suited for the case where there are large differences in home range size, but small or no differences in probability of detection for individuals with activity centers at a detector, between two groups of individuals (often sexes), but group membership is not observed (i.e. sex is unknown).  If this is the case with your data, I don't see specific reasons to suspect problems with results from your a0 parameterizations.  Looking at coefficients for model 5, it's interesting that such a high fraction of the individuals fall into the group with larger sigma... was the study area small relative to bears home range size?  If so, you might expect a male-biased sample due to their greater movement rates, and hence a large number of animals in the 2nd mixture with larger sigma(?).

If you have a reasonable number of recaptures, results from models with and without individual heterogeneity shouldn't produce drastically different estimates. I think the low AIC weight and high and imprecise estimate of N from your model 3 is good evidence that the model doesn't fit your data well. I don't think that means that the a0 is better for modeling IH generally.  The parameter estimates for the effect of belonging to the second mixture in Howe et al. are quite precise and based on a large sample, and I also have a just so story that could explain the pattern we found... I'd like to think that we wouldn't have found support for the a0 parameterization with out data, but I can't be sure.

I agree that it would be nice to be able to try models with different pmix for the different parameters.

How small is your data set?  What is the ratio of detections to individuals?  Do you have the sex information?

All the best,
Eric

messages.author: 2c49652a5796ed9c
messages.subject: Re: compensatory heterogeneity and finite mixture models
parts:
Upon further reflection, the coefficients in models 3 and 5 are not necessarily in contradiction.  In the a0 parameterization, increasing sigma indirectly increases g0 and reducing a0 indirectly decreases g0 and we'd have to do some math to see if it is a net gain or loss.  Perhaps the moral to the story is that ignoring individual heterogeneity can be not that problematic or very problematic depending on the amount of compensation and modeling heterogeneity appropriately might be tricky business.

Ben

messages.author: 0dbfcf0efe4ff8fe
messages.subject: Re: compensatory heterogeneity and finite mixture models
parts:
OK, males only and plenty of recaptures...

My take on the finite mixtures is the coefficients are rarely "correct".  Detectability may vary among individuals due to many different factors; the two groups are forced because we use the 2-point mixture distribution to model the heterogeneity and may have no biological meaning at all.  When the coefficients for one of the mixtures really don't make sense (e.g. extremely low and imprecise g0 or sigma, as can occur with a high proportion of single captures), I usually conclude that the data "can't support" the mixture distribution and present estimates from a model that ignores heterogeneity, cautioning that D and N may have been underestimated and confidence interval coverage is likely less than nominal.  However, you seem to have both support for, and sufficient data to model, the heterogeneity.  Even if the coefficients don't correspond to real groups of animals, you can avoid negative bias and false precision by modeling the heterogeneity.

Even for your fairly large data set, you have included a lot of effects in your models.  Most effects are similar under different heterogeneity parameterizations, but we see that most of the parameter estimates change somewhat.  This situation makes it even riskier to try to infer too much from the coefficients, but I think it's reasonable to assume that your population estimates are useful (good chance that the true value is within the 95% CI), and in addition you've demonstrated some interesting effects (e.g. of area, in response to previous capture).  Will you be doing any model-averaging of the coefficients or abundance estimates?

Eric

messages.author: ac711cfc7e742bce
messages.subject: Re: compensatory heterogeneity and finite mixture models
parts:
I replied to Eric, but forgot to reply all to the rest of the group.

I agree that we can't really interpret the two classes of the finite mixture model, but it's nice to have a biologically plausible explanation.  Of course these are easy to generate, so maybe they're not that useful.  The original cause for concern was finite mixture parameters that were inconsistent between g0 and a0 parameterizations.  When you increase sigma in the a0 parameterization, you indirectly decrease g0.  When you increase sigma in the g0 parameterization, you increase g0.  I fit these models to another male and female data set and it didn't produce the contradictory estimates.  In one case, there appeared to be some compensation and in the other case, not.  In the process, I managed to confuse myself about the original problem.  The original estimates are indeed contradictory.  Because of this and the poor performance of finite mixtures in small data sets with low capture probabilities in general, I think we'll ignore individual heterogeneity and say our estimates are probably conservative.  We are model averaging to shrink study area effects back towards a common mean.

None of these 3 data sets were very large.  I don't think you necessarily need a large data set to detect heterogeneity, but you may need a large data set to model it appropriately.  I wonder to what extent the Curse of Link remains in spatial mark recapture.  Instead of trying to correctly identify one heterogeneity distribution, we're now trying to correctly identify two potentially correlated random effects.
